items.t: Anthropic closes first day of trading about 17% above IPO price after record $81.3bn listing
items.s: Anthropic, the startup behind the Claude chatbot, ended its first day of US trading about 17% above its offer price. The Guardian reported that the listing raised $81.3bn, surpassing the previous record set by SpaceX.
p: Anthropic’s shares closed at just over $97 on Thursday, according to the Guardian, compared with an initial public offering price of $83. The stock had reached an early high of $111.50 and rose 34% when trading opened, a move that briefly valued the company at more than $2tn.

At the close, the company had a total market capitalisation of nearly $1.3tn, or $1.75tn on a fully diluted basis. The Guardian reported that Anthropic’s chief executive, Dario Amodei, rang the Nasdaq opening bell.

Anthropic announced late on Wednesday that it had sold 980m shares to underwriters in an upsized offering. The Guardian said the deal raised $81.3bn, beating SpaceX’s initial $75bn fundraise in June, and described the listing as one of the biggest stock market flotations in history.

The broader market was less enthusiastic. US stocks slumped at the end of trading, and most major chipmakers closed lower than they opened. Nvidia extended its losses to a sixth day after its latest earnings call, while Micron and Broadcom also saw their shares decline.

Analysts at Yorkville Ives said Anthropic is the first firm focused entirely on its field to be publicly traded, and wrote that the listing could help restore investor confidence. Evan Schlossman, a principal at Neostellar, said investors will focus on whether the company’s growth rate can be sustained once it is public.

According to its investor prospectus, filed at the end of October, Anthropic brought in $16.2bn in revenue in the first six months of 2026, up from $4.6bn for all of 2025. The company also reported losses of $80bn in the first half, which it said were largely due to a one-off charge, and losses of $104bn over the first nine months.

Computing power, supplied by arrays of semiconductor chips often housed in datacenters, was Anthropic’s largest single expense, at about $18.8bn in the first nine months of 2026. The executives wrote in the prospectus that they expect costs to balloon as the company secures more of it.

The Guardian also noted that Anthropic has detailed in its filings how its technology could pose dangers, including being used to develop bioweapons, and that Amodei has called for a slowdown in the development of the most advanced systems. The listing comes as the industry braces for possible fallout from a recent Nvidia scandal that led to the resignation of its chief executive, Jensen Huang.
items.cav: This account rests on a single outlet, and the revenue and loss figures are taken from the company’s prospectus as reported, not from independent verification. The Nvidia scandal and Huang’s resignation are mentioned only in passing, without detail on what happened.
items.op: A public listing is only as credible as the disclosures behind it. Investors can now weigh Anthropic’s $104bn in losses against its revenue, and that scrutiny is exactly what transparency should invite. Regulators and reporters should keep demanding audited, consistent figures rather than accepting the upbeat headline.

items.t: European leaders say they are ready for talks with Russia to end the war in Ukraine
items.s: At a Berlin summit of Ukraine’s allies, European leaders said they were ready to negotiate with Russia, but Moscow has given mixed signals on whether Europe will get a seat at the table.
p: European leaders said at a summit in Berlin that they were ready for negotiations with Russia to end the war in Ukraine, in a show of support for Kyiv. The gathering of Ukraine’s allies, known as the Coalition of the Willing, was reported by the BBC.

According to the BBC, UK Prime Minister Andy Burnham said Europe had a “clear and consistent and united negotiating position.” German Chancellor Friedrich Merz said Moscow’s maximalist demands were not realistic, and that serious talks with Russia on European security should be matched by a peace agreement with Ukraine first.

The summit followed historic trilateral talks in Shenzhen, in south-eastern China, between Donald Trump, Vladimir Putin and Chinese President Xi Jinping. Trump joined the Berlin summit by phone from Air Force One, the report said.

Jared Kushner, one of two US envoys in Berlin, said Trump had come away from Shenzhen believing that peace was achievable. He said the Russians were willing for Europeans to be at the table, and that Moscow was “comfortable” with Ukraine receiving security guarantees modelled on Nato’s Article Five.

Putin said at a press conference after the talks that Russia was not against European participation but wanted to know what Europe would bring. He said Moscow had invited Europeans to Moscow to clarify their positions. He also said Russia was not planning to attack anyone, and questioned talk in Europe of war coming in 2030.

Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelensky, Merz and French President Emmanuel Macron were less optimistic. Zelensky said Putin had always said no to proposals so far. Macron urged allies to do the maximum to deliver air defence systems to Kyiv and called for the question of Ukraine’s Nato membership to be reopened. Reports say US negotiators have considered Article Five-style guarantees for Ukraine without Nato membership, if Kyiv agreed to painful territorial concessions.

The Russian position remains unclear. US envoys Steve Witkoff and Kushner had appeared certain after a Moscow visit that Europe would soon have a seat, but Putin’s aide Yury Ushakov said a great deal would have to be done before the format could expand.

On the same day, drones struck several buildings in Kyiv’s historic centre. One person was killed in a strike on a residential building in the Podilskyi neighbourhood, and the Dutch and Austrian embassies and Saint Volodymyr’s Cathedral reported damage. Putin vowed that Moscow’s response to a Ukrainian strike on the Crimean Bridge would be “considerably more painful,” and said he had discussed a possible ceasefire but decided against it after that attack.
items.cav: Putin’s claims and the US envoys’ upbeat assessments are the statements of the parties themselves and are not independently confirmed. Reports about possible guarantees without Nato membership are second-hand, and the sources do not say what happened in the Crimean Bridge attack or who carried it out.
items.op: Peace talks cannot be built on understandings struck between great powers while the country under attack is kept at the edge of the room. Any settlement that trades Ukrainian territory or security without Kyiv’s full consent would reward the party that rejected every offer so far. Governments should publish what is being discussed in Shenzhen and Berlin.

items.t: UN top court finds Myanmar committed genocide against Rohingya in 2017 crackdown
items.s: The International Court of Justice has ruled that Myanmar committed genocide against its Rohingya minority, the first time the court has held a state responsible for the crime. The finding concerns a 2017 military crackdown in Rakhine State.
p: The UN’s highest court, the International Court of Justice (ICJ), has concluded that Myanmar carried out genocide against the Rohingya, according to the BBC and a French broadcaster. Both reports describe the Thursday decision as unprecedented, since no international court had previously held a state responsible for genocide in this way.

ICJ president Yuji Iwasawa said Myanmar acted with an “intention to destroy” a large part of the Rohingya population and destroyed evidence on a wide scale to conceal its conduct. As the BBC relayed his remarks, he described indiscriminate killings, executions of men, widespread sexual violence, severe violence against children and the deliberate burning of Rohingya homes, as well as attacks on people fleeing to Bangladesh.

The judgement was reached by a majority of nine votes to six. The court also found that Myanmar had breached several other provisions of the 1948 Genocide Convention. The French broadcaster said the panel of 15 judges had spent seven years weighing the case, which The Gambia brought against Myanmar.

The reports give different figures for the scale of the violence. The BBC said the ICJ determined that around 10,000 Rohingya were killed during the operation and that about 815,000 had been targeted in some way, with more than 700,000 thought to have fled to Bangladesh. The French report spoke of thousands of killings and said at least 700,000 people were driven out of Myanmar.

Myanmar has rejected the genocide claims throughout, saying its operations targeted militant threats after attacks by the Arakan Rohingya Salvation Army. Its representative, Ko Ko Hlaing, told the court in January that the state could not stand by while “terrorists” roamed freely. After the ruling he declined to comment, the BBC reported.

The French report noted that Min Aung Hlaing, who commanded the military during the crackdown, later ousted the elected government in a 2021 coup. This year he was installed as civilian president after heavily restricted elections. The ICJ has no means of enforcing its rulings, but the finding is likely to add diplomatic pressure on him.

According to the BBC, the court said Myanmar must pay proportionate reparations, though the exact amount could be set later. Rohingya communities and human rights groups welcomed the decision. UN human rights chief Volker Türk described the suffering of the Rohingya as a stain on humanity’s conscience and urged that the ruling lead to concrete action.

Mohammed Nowkim, a Rohingya who fled Rakhine in 2017 and now lives in Canada, told the BBC that the verdict amounted to a formal acknowledgment of what his community endured. Legal observers will also watch a separate ICJ case, brought by South Africa, which accuses Israel of genocide against Palestinians in Gaza, for signs of how the court approaches such claims.
items.cav: The reports give different casualty and displacement figures, with the BBC citing about 10,000 killed and the French report citing thousands, so the precise toll is not settled by these sources. Survivor accounts are reported as testimony and have not been independently verified here.
items.op: The verdict matters because it tests whether the Genocide Convention means anything when the state itself is accused. Recognition alone is not justice: reparations, prosecutions and open access to evidence must follow, or the ruling will remain words on paper.

items.t: European leaders reject ‘Yalta 2.0’ for Ukraine after Trump, Putin and Xi talks
items.s: European leaders have rejected any attempt to repeat the 1945 Yalta Conference over Ukraine, a day after Donald Trump, Vladimir Putin and Xi Jinping met in China. Berlin hosted a parallel gathering of Kyiv’s backers.
p: Continental leaders are pushing back against any effort to revive the logic of the 1945 Yalta Conference as a way to end Russia’s war, according to Euronews. The concern is that such an arrangement would carve Europe into zones of influence.

The objection surfaced on Thursday at a session of the Coalition of the Willing, a grouping of Kyiv’s allies, convened in Berlin by Chancellor Friedrich Merz. It followed by only a few hours a trilateral encounter in Shenzhen between Putin, Trump and Xi, which commentators have labelled “Yalta 2.0”.
Although the three leaders discussed Ukraine, the joint text they issued, called “Declaration Toward Peace”, made no reference to the country, the report said.

Merz argued that a Yalta-style arrangement would not produce peace, and pledged that Europe would not accept a repeat of such a division. French President Emmanuel Macron said the Shenzhen statement, which contained four points, did not mirror the 1945 outcome that preceded the Cold War. He insisted that any negotiation must bring Ukraine, Europe, the United States and Russia to the same table.

British Prime Minister Andy Burnham supported that stance, holding that Ukraine cannot be decided on without Ukraine present. Volodymyr Zelenskyy, the Ukrainian president, read the Berlin meeting as evidence that Moscow had not managed to split European allies.

According to the report, the four leaders agreed that Europe should now hold direct talks with Russia, a step not yet taken. Europe has named a joint team of seven envoys, drawn from France, Britain, Germany, Poland, Italy, the EU institutions and NATO, for the next round. US envoys Steve Witkoff and Jared Kushner, who travelled to Berlin, also urged Russia to accept European participation.

Putin, speaking in Shenzhen, said he had proposed through diplomatic channels that Europeans travel to Moscow to set out their positions, after which the Kremlin would decide whether to continue dialogue with Kyiv. He also questioned discussing Europe’s security without Europe. Macron described Moscow’s demands on the continent’s security structure as excessive.

Merz said that debate on European security would only follow a settled peace in Ukraine. Guarantees under discussion include a clause modelled on NATO’s collective defence provision in case Russia attacks again, and a European-led peacekeeping force, which Putin has said he would reject in any case. Kushner called an Article 5-style guarantee a significant step that Trump might accept if it served American interests.

Kushner confirmed that Trump joined the closed-door Berlin discussions by phone from his aircraft. Media reports suggest Trump voiced doubts about Europe’s military support for Ukraine, yet the leaders present seemed unmoved and agreed that assistance would continue.
items.cav: The account rests on a single outlet’s reporting. Trump’s scepticism about European military support comes from unnamed media reports, and the guarantees and peacekeeping force remain under discussion without final terms.
items.op: Europe is right to insist that decisions on its security are made with Europe and Ukraine at the table. A joint statement that does not even name Ukraine is a poor basis for peace, and deals made over the heads of the affected countries should never be presented as settlements. Transparent, rule-based talks are the only durable route.

items.t: Trump leaves China without meeting Kim Jong-un as three-way summit raises concerns across Asia
items.s: US President Donald Trump departed China without the Kim Jong-un encounter he had sought, while a rare summit with Xi Jinping and Vladimir Putin left South Korea, Japan and Taiwan uneasy about being sidelined.
p: Trump flew out of Shenzhen on Thursday with no meeting held with the North Korean leader, despite having pursued one during the trip. The stop was built around a seldom-seen gathering of Trump, Xi and Putin on the fringes of the Asia-Pacific Economic Cooperation summit.

Trump had raised the idea of a Kim meeting many times, though a White House official had said none was scheduled. On Monday he told reporters at the White House that a encounter with Kim might still happen, calling that prospect welcome.
Kim, for his part, was reported by the South Korean agency Newsis to have toured locations in North Korea’s South Hamgyong province on Tuesday and Wednesday.

The three leaders committed to continuing talks on reducing nuclear risks and curbing proliferation. Their joint declaration, however, never named the Korean Peninsula or Taiwan. Xinhua, China’s state news agency, later indicated that the leaders had compared notes on the peninsula, Ukraine, nuclear non-proliferation and the Middle East.

Concern in South Korea, Japan and Taiwan centres on the worry that big powers might settle matters touching their security without involving them. Seoul’s media drew comparisons with the 1945 Yalta Conference. Money Today, a South Korean outlet, argued that leaving the peninsula out eased fears of a repeat but suggested denuclearisation is losing ground on the diplomatic agenda. Park Won-gon of Ewha Womans University thought China and Russia might have taken Pyongyang’s side, while Kim Jae-chun of Sogang University saw the three powers as far apart on North Korea’s nuclear programme. Newsis argued that the lack of a Trump-Kim meeting for a second year could reduce worries about Washington recognising North Korea as a nuclear-armed state. President Lee Jae-myung, speaking at APEC, again stressed peace and stability on the peninsula.

Japan’s Prime Minister Sanae Takaichi greeted Xi at APEC, but the two held no formal talks. A ruling-party lawmaker told Fuji TV that Japan’s exclusion could look like a diplomatic setback. Takaichi told reporters in Shenzhen she did not think Japan’s interests would suffer, according to TBS. Citing government sources, TV Asahi reported she is setting up a call with Trump.

The declaration also asked for respect for the immunity of state officials and warned that the International Criminal Court and similar bodies must not overreach. The court is currently led by Japanese judge Tomoko Akane. It issued an arrest warrant for Putin in March 2023 over the alleged unlawful deportation of Ukrainian children. Japanese media drew attention to this passage.

In Taiwan, TVBS warned the island could become a bargaining chip. Taiwan came up in the Xi-Trump talks earlier on Thursday. Tsai Jung-hsiang of National Chung Cheng University told the Central News Agency that Washington and Beijing read strategic stability very differently, and that Xi wants Washington to accept Beijing’s claim over sovereignty. Tsai said he expects no shift in US Taiwan policy from the meeting.
Chinese state media presented the three-way meeting as a chance for the major powers to cooperate on international security and stability.
items.cav: The sources disagree on whether the Korean Peninsula was discussed: the joint declaration does not mention it, while Xinhua says the leaders exchanged views on it. Kim’s activities, Trump’s plans and Takaichi’s planned call rest on Newsis, the White House and Japanese government sources reported by others. Most analysis is second-hand from South Korean, Japanese and Taiwanese outlets.
items.op: A summit that reshapes regional security should not be settled in closed rooms. When a joint declaration says nothing about the Korean Peninsula or Taiwan, while the people there watch the outcome, transparency is the minimum owed. Leaders who discuss the fate of others should explain their terms in public.

items.t: Trump Reportedly Challenges Europe’s Ukraine Spending in Unannounced Call
items.s: US President Donald Trump reportedly joined a gathering of Kyiv’s European backers by phone and pressed them on the cost of their military help. The account rests on European officials who spoke to Politico.
p: According to Politico, Trump has “sharply questioned” European governments about their ongoing funding for Ukraine as it fights Russia. The outlet said four European officials who were briefed on the exchange provided the details.

The call reportedly came on Thursday, without warning, as Trump asked why Europe was still putting vast sums into arms for Kyiv. It followed a session in Shenzhen, China, where he had met Vladimir Putin and Xi Jinping.

Three of the officials, who spoke on condition of anonymity, said Trump doubted that the Coalition of the Willing could deliver more assistance. The grouping includes 34 nations along with Ukraine. One official said Trump lamented the loss of life and argued that funds were being squandered in a conflict that has dragged on for close to five years.

The same official said Trump believes Putin is prepared to work toward a settlement with Kyiv. Trump is said to have made these remarks while aboard Air Force One, insisting that the Russian leader was serious about negotiating.
items.cav: Every detail comes second-hand from anonymous European officials cited by Politico, and the evidence contains no direct White House statement. The summary says Moscow is ready to negotiate, while the article attributes that view to Trump’s own reading of Putin, so Russia’s actual position remains unsettled.
items.op: Decisions about billions in public money and the future of an invaded nation should not be shaped by unannounced calls and anonymous briefings. Allies and voters deserve on-the-record positions from Washington. If peace talks are the goal, open statements about what is being demanded, and from whom, are the minimum standard.

items.t: Trump, Xi and Putin hold unprecedented Shenzhen meeting without announced nuclear deal
items.s: The presidents of the United States, China and Russia met on Thursday in Shenzhen, on the sidelines of the Apec summit, for a first-of-its-kind trilateral gathering. It ended without an announced breakthrough on the main issues, though the three sides issued a joint declaration.
p: The session lasted more than an hour and covered nuclear weapons, the war in Ukraine and wider international security. Donald Trump opened by telling Xi Jinping and Vladimir Putin that “we are really making history”, describing the three countries as “uniquely positioned” to discuss reducing their nuclear stockpiles.

The backdrop is the New Start treaty, which limits the deployed strategic nuclear warheads of the US and Russia and expires in February. Putin had proposed voluntarily keeping those limits for another year. Trump rejected that approach and called instead for a new agreement that would include China.

At the meeting, Xi called for every effort to prevent nuclear war and for nuclear weapons to be completely prohibited and destroyed. No new arms control agreement was announced. Putin said the three countries had many converging interests in resolving conflicts, and he named Ukraine specifically.

A joint “peace declaration”, released by Chinese and Russian state media, called for reform of the United Nations and dialogue on reducing nuclear risks. According to reports, it also reaffirmed the importance of stable energy flows, a theme that follows months of disruption linked to the Iran conflict and the Strait of Hormuz.

Ukraine appears to have been a secondary topic. A Kremlin spokesperson said it was not the central subject of the trilateral talks, and Kyiv was not mentioned in the declaration. Trump also reportedly urged Xi to help resolve the war, and the reports differ on how much the Iran war featured in the meeting.

The declaration also criticised the International Criminal Court, saying the court and similar bodies “must not abuse their jurisdiction”. Trump had earlier called the court “out of control”. The ICC issued an arrest warrant for Putin in March 2023, accusing him of unlawfully deporting Ukrainian children. The US and China are not parties to the Rome statute.
Trump has invited Putin to the G20 summit in Miami next month. Reports say European G20 members have made clear they do not want to share a room with him, and Putin has skipped recent G20 summits.
items.cav: The Guardian reports no announced breakthrough, while the joint declaration’s contents reached the public mainly through Chinese and Russian state media. Accounts differ on whether Iran was discussed, and the Kremlin’s description of Ukraine’s place in the talks is its own. Trump’s claim that Xi agreed on the Strait of Hormuz is unverified.
items.op: Summit theatre is cheap; the measure is whether nuclear limits are written down before New Start lapses. A declaration that questions an international court while a leader named in its arrest warrant sits at the table should worry anyone who believes accountability for war crimes must apply to the powerful. Transparency should be demanded of the promised dialogue.

items.t: UN top court rules Myanmar committed genocide against the Rohingya
items.s: The International Court of Justice has ruled, by nine votes to six, that Myanmar committed genocide against the Rohingya. It is the first time the court has found a state responsible for the crime.
p: The ruling concerns the military campaign of 2017 in northern Rakhine State. Court president Yuji Iwasawa read the verdict in The Hague, and said the judges found that Myanmar’s security forces had killed thousands of Rohingya civilians, committed widespread sexual violence and inflicted extreme violence on children. He also said attacks on fleeing Rohingya had been part of the campaign.

Sources differ on the scale of the flight. The Guardian and NPR-style summaries point to hundreds of thousands who crossed into Bangladesh, while Al Jazeera put the number at more than 730,000. According to Al Jazeera, Iwasawa said evidence showed Myanmar forces had killed 10,000 Rohingya, a figure the other outlets do not repeat.

The judges said the only reasonable inference from the evidence was an intention to destroy a substantial part of the Rohingya population. Genocide is a demanding legal test, and lawyers note that intent is the hardest element to prove. The court also found that the Rohingya form a distinct ethnic group under international law, a status Myanmar has denied, referring to them as Bengalis or foreign migrants.

The court ordered Myanmar to pay reparations for the damage caused, although the amount will be set later. It also called for the safe and voluntary return of refugees, the return or replacement of collective property, help in finding the disappeared, and rehabilitation for survivors. Myanmar was told to investigate and, where necessary, prosecute those suspected of taking part.

Reaction was swift. Britain said it would expel Myanmar’s defence attaché in London and asked for a session of the UN Security Council. Amnesty International’s secretary general, Agnes Callamard, welcomed the verdict as a rare moment of justice. Rohingya survivors in Bangladesh, some of whom watched the reading on outdoor screens, expressed relief, but several said their fight was not over.

The ICJ’s rulings are binding and cannot be appealed, but the court has no power to enforce them. It is unclear whether Myanmar’s leaders will comply. Min Aung Hlaing, who led the military during the 2017 crackdown and was later installed as civilian president after elections critics called tightly restricted, faces pressure from the ruling. Myanmar has consistently denied committing genocide, saying it was responding to militant attacks.

Legal observers are also watching the case for its bearing on South Africa’s separate genocide case against Israel over Gaza. More than a million Rohingya still live in refugee camps in Bangladesh, according to the UN.
items.cav: Sources differ on the number who fled (hundreds of thousands versus more than 730,000) and on the death toll, with only Al Jazeera reporting a figure of 10,000. The reparations amount has not been set, and no immediate response from Myanmar’s government or military was reported. Claims about possible US sanctions on ICJ judges were reported by only one outlet and remain a prediction.
items.op: A landmark verdict is only as strong as the steps that follow it, and this court cannot enforce its own judgment. Myanmar’s leaders should be judged by whether refugees can return safely, reparations are paid and suspects face investigation. The world should not let this ruling become another document gathering dust.

items.t: After Democrats win the House and Senate, columnists urge vigilance against further democratic backsliding
items.s: Writing after the US midterm elections, Congressman Steve Cohen and Michael Shank argue that the Democratic gains do not end the threat to American democratic institutions. They say the danger will persist, and that state, local and congressional actors must stay alert.
p: Cohen and Shank say the midterms produced a wave of historic firsts across several states, including the country’s first female Black governor, its first female Native American governor and its first Muslim US senator. They also say voters rejected the agenda of President Donald Trump, and that Democrats now hold the majority in both chambers of Congress.

The authors argue that this result will not stop what they describe as anti-democratic behaviour. They say the White House has already laid out a plan to govern for the next two years without Congress, through more executive orders, more vetoes and more legal delays. They also expect Republicans to pursue retribution during the lame-duck session, including one final reconciliation bill passed without Democratic input.

Cohen and Shank list several actions by the administration before the vote. According to their account, it offered $1 million for reports of voter fraud and $5,000 bribes tied to midterm results, suggested without evidence that China was meddling in elections, tried to thwart mail-in voting, and pressed states to segregate ballots. The column does not supply independent documentation for these claims.

The writers say such behaviour may escalate in the coming months, possibly under cover of an escalated war on Iran. They do not explain in detail how that conflict would affect domestic politics, and they warn that a White House move toward emergency declarations, power outages or martial law would change the picture.

They urge state and local officials, who they say prepared for worst-case scenarios, not to relax. The column points to the Mayors Innovation Project and other groups that have given local leaders emergency management plans, which the groups describe as a starting point rather than a complete solution.

Cohen and Shank also highlight grassroots networks such as Defend 612 in Minneapolis, which they say has an 80,000-strong network, and Free DC in Washington, which they say has thousands of trained members. They cite a report called The American Crisis, which calls local communities the “central locus of control” in stabilising the country’s democratic transition, and they call on Congress to take its constitutional oath seriously when it convenes in January.

The authors conclude that the work ahead is much larger than a single election day or swearing-in ceremony, and that the new Congress should work with local movements. They present the current mobilisation as a sign of renewed civic engagement, though they acknowledge it was prompted by a serious threat.
items.cav: This is an opinion column, and one author is a sitting member of Congress, so its framing is advocacy rather than reporting. Figures such as the $1 million reward, the $5,000 payments, the 80,000-member network and the claims about Iran are the authors’ own assertions and are not sourced in the text. The piece was published after the midterms and does not report official responses from the White House.
items.op: Democratic gains do not restore the checks that were strained during this campaign. The stakes are the credibility of future elections and the rule of law itself. Officials at every level should treat vigilance as a standing duty, not a seasonal response to a crisis.

items.t: US and Venezuela restore military ties under interim government less than a year after Maduro’s seizure
items.s: Washington and Venezuela’s interim authorities have signed a military co-operation agreement, less than a year after US forces seized Nicolás Maduro. Few details of the deal have been made public.
p: Less than a year after American forces captured Nicolás Maduro in an operation in Caracas, Washington and Venezuela have moved to renew their military relationship, according to BBC News.

The interim government, headed by Delcy Rodríguez, who previously served as Maduro’s vice-president, signed the accord with US Defence Secretary Pete Hegseth on Wednesday. Hegseth praised the change, saying Venezuela had shifted from being Washington’s most aggressive regional threat to a “compliant security partner” in under a year.

The two countries had cut military links back in 2005, when Hugo Chávez ended cooperation. Chávez claimed that American personnel sent to train Venezuelan soldiers had insulted his government, and he accused a US military office at Fuerte Tiuna, the country’s largest military base, of working as a CIA arm.

Ties then worsened under Maduro, who took over after Chávez died of cancer. Tensions peaked late last year, when Washington doubled its reward for information leading to Maduro’s arrest to $50m. US forces took him on 3 January, and he and his wife, Cilia Flores, are now held in New York on drug-trafficking and conspiracy charges, which they reject.

Rodríguez called the agreement highly significant for bilateral relations. She spoke of training for Venezuela’s armed forces, upgrades to their equipment and access to new technology, all aimed at tackling shared dangers. Nothing has been published about the specifics.

Speaking at the US embassy in Caracas, Hegseth was blunter about who he regards as the enemy. He told narco-terrorists who use Venezuela as a refuge that they would be pursued and killed, and he quoted Maduro’s own prediction that the raid would bring peace rather than war.

Hegseth then travelled to Colombia, whose president, Abelardo de la Espriella, is a close ally of the Trump administration. Colombia already belongs to the US-led Americas Counter Cartel Coalition, and in August Hegseth had raised the idea of joint US-Colombian operations against armed groups. On Wednesday, De la Espriella publicly denied a New York Times report that he had turned down such operations, saying any decision would respect Colombia’s constitution, laws and sovereignty. Hegseth responded online that the partnership was stronger than ever.
items.cav: The agreement’s contents have not been published, so claims about its scope rest on speeches by Hegseth and Rodríguez. The New York Times report on Colombia is second-hand, and De la Espriella disputes it; the sources do not independently verify either account.
items.op: A military pact struck without published terms asks the public to trust announcements over documents. Any deal that shapes armed operations across borders should face parliamentary scrutiny and open examination. Secrecy over the details is the real danger here.

items.t: Xi, Putin and Trump Meet in Shenzhen and Agree a “Peace Declaration”
items.s: Leaders of China, Russia and the United States held a three-way meeting in Shenzhen and endorsed a declaration that nuclear war must never be fought. The text also covers UN reform, fuel supplies and the legal shield for state officials.
p: Xi Jinping, Vladimir Putin and Donald Trump sat down together on Thursday in Shenzhen, in southern China, a gathering the participants have called a first of its kind. China and Russia say the three agreed a “peace declaration” restating that nuclear conflict should be ruled out.

Beyond the nuclear language, the document commits the signatories to pushing for changes at the United Nations, to expanding the flow of refined oil products to every country, and to preserving the protections that state officials hold before international tribunals. Xinhua and the Kremlin both published the text.

The meeting came at the end of a three-day Asian tour for Trump, which the report describes as delivering little concrete progress despite his claims to be making history and mediating peace. He flew home without speaking to reporters after the talks. Earlier he had met Xi and Putin one-on-one and called each of them a friend.

Putin's presence is the most contentious part of the picture. The International Criminal Court in The Hague has sought his arrest, along with five other Russian officials. He and Maria Lvova-Belova, Russia's children's commissioner, face allegations of unlawfully moving Ukrainian children out of the country, and the remaining warrants concern alleged war crimes and crimes against humanity linked to the full-scale invasion. Moscow denies all of it.

Jonathan Eyal of the RUSI think tank in London said the challenge to international courts and norms was the most striking element. In his view, Putin came away with legitimacy and a way out of pariah status, whereas Trump received a publicity moment that was not needed.

Putin arrived after a blow to his war effort, when a key bridge connecting Crimea to Russia was put out of action. He said the three countries share many interests in resolving regional disputes, Ukraine above all. Xi avoided naming Ukraine, instead arguing that peace follows when great powers cooperate and that clashes bring turmoil. He also urged Washington to act responsibly on Taiwan to avoid serious damage to the relationship.

The three governments remain far apart on Ukraine, Iran, nuclear arms and trade, which the report says makes a lasting result uncertain. Japanese Prime Minister Sanae Takaichi received no formal welcome and was described as isolated during the summit. Relations between Tokyo and Beijing have deteriorated since her 2025 comments that Japan could use its armed forces if a Chinese action against Taiwan endangered Japanese territory. She maintained that Tokyo's stance on Taiwan has stayed the same since 1972. Smaller states, worried their own interests could be ignored, have reacted with unease.
items.cav: The declaration's contents are known only from the statements of China and Russia and from the texts they released; the account does not say what the US agreed to, and Trump offered no comment. Claims that the meeting was historic come from the leaders themselves. The Ukraine remarks and Eyal's analysis are the outlet's reporting and were not independently verified.
items.op: A pledge to protect the immunity of officials in international courts, made by a leader under an ICC arrest warrant, deserves scrutiny rather than applause. Accountability for alleged war crimes should not be bargained away in a summit photo. Diplomacy with Moscow is legitimate, but it must not quietly erode the rules meant to hold the powerful to account.

items.t: Guardian writer warns parents off Grand Theft Auto VI, citing sex, drugs and violence
items.s: A Guardian writer who has spent more than 70 hours with Rockstar Games’ Grand Theft Auto VI says the 18-rated game is not suitable for children. The column argues that parents often misread what an 18 rating covers.
p: The game, released this week according to the column, is set in a virtual Florida and follows two fugitives, Jason and Lucia, through a series of crimes. The writer describes it as a technical achievement and says it is often funny and, at times, unexpectedly moving, particularly through the central love story between the two characters.

The main objection is content. The writer says players steal cars, run and sell drugs, shoot police and rival criminals, and kill hundreds of people over the course of the story. The column also describes executions, brutal police raids and depictions of torture.

The writer says the sexual content is more explicit than in any earlier Grand Theft Auto title. Among the examples given are full-frontal nudity, a mission set during a pornographic shoot, several scenes in strip clubs and bars, and a browsable in-game version of OnlyFans on one character’s laptop. The column recalls that 2004’s Grand Theft Auto: San Andreas was briefly pulled from sale over a sex minigame that was hidden in the code.

Drug use is also central, the writer says. Party scenes involving cocaine are common, and the player can take part. The column adds that much of the in-game radio, podcasts and street dialogue is crude, with sexual and bodily humour throughout.

The writer, who is a parent of two boys aged 10 and seven, says the game is not material they would want to see or hear. The column recounts an earlier episode in which a child asked to play Grand Theft Auto V at a birthday party, and says the child’s mother was surprised to learn that an 18 rating signals adult content rather than difficulty.

The writer says the piece is not a call for a moral panic about adult games and that the content is fair game for adults. The sources available do not include a response from Rockstar Games, and the column’s account of the game’s content is one reviewer’s personal experience rather than an independent audit.
items.cav: This is a single opinion column, not a news report, and it gives no response from Rockstar Games. The claim that ratings boards share the writer’s view is asserted, not sourced, and the writer’s account of 2004 and the 2014 party is personal recollection.
items.op: Age ratings only work if parents understand what they signal, and this column shows how easily that understanding breaks down. Publishers that sell explicit adult games should make content warnings clear and specific. Parents deserve plain information before they buy, not a label they have to decode.

items.t: Danish parliament ratifies Arctic security pact with US and Greenland
items.s: Denmark’s parliament has unanimously approved a new security agreement between Greenland, Denmark and the United States, easing a long dispute over US President Donald Trump’s stated ambition to control the Arctic territory. Danish officials say the deal is a step toward rebuilding trust, though questions about future US bases remain open.
p: The Folketing, Denmark’s parliament, approved the agreement on Thursday after its second reading. Reports say all 109 lawmakers present voted for it, with no votes against and no debate. Greenland’s own parliament had already approved the text earlier in November, by 16 votes with seven abstentions, according to Euronews.

The pact was signed in September after months of talks by Trump and the prime ministers of Greenland and Denmark, Jens-Frederik Nielsen and Mette Frederiksen. Euronews says the signing took place in New York on 22 September. The agreement updates a 1951 defence accord and gives the US underwater access to Greenland, as well as specific permission to build a missile defence system.

The text also treats Greenland, a former Danish colony, as an equal partner. Under its terms, Greenland would remain in NATO if it ever became fully independent of Denmark. Euronews adds that the deal lets the US build two new military bases on the island, and that it shuts out countries outside the EU and NATO from strategic sectors, an effort aimed at limiting Chinese or Russian influence, particularly through investment.

Danish Foreign Minister Lars Løkke Rasmussen said the ratification settled Denmark’s side of the process and removed uncertainty about Greenland’s future. He also acknowledged that trust in the US had suffered, and said repairing it would be a significant task, to be carried out within the agreement’s framework.

Løkke Rasmussen said that as of Thursday the US had not told Denmark of any plans to set up new military bases, even though Trump had earlier said the US would quickly begin building a large military presence in an appropriate part of Greenland.

The US ambassador to Denmark, Ken Howery, welcomed the vote and said the agreement would strengthen the security of the United States, the Kingdom of Denmark, including Greenland, and NATO as a whole. Relations between Washington, Copenhagen, Greenland and the alliance had come under severe strain during repeated threats by Trump to take over the territory.

The Guardian reports that the pact still needs one final step: Trump must notify the US Congress before it takes effect. The paper also reports, citing earlier reports, that Copenhagen sent blood bags and explosives for blowing up runways in January, as it prepared for a possible US invasion. Those details come second-hand and the paper does not confirm them independently.
items.cav: The sources differ on the base question: Euronews says the deal allows two new US bases, while Løkke Rasmussen said Denmark had not been told of any base plans. The January preparations are only reported, and the timing of the US congressional notification is not confirmed.
items.op: A security deal reached under the shadow of threats to invade an ally should be judged by its transparency. Denmark and Greenland should publish every US base plan and the congressional notice in full. Trust cannot be rebuilt by treaty text alone; it requires that Washington’s commitments be verifiable.

items.t: Trump, Xi and Putin Hold First Trilateral Meeting at Shenzhen APEC Summit
items.s: Donald Trump, Xi Jinping and Vladimir Putin met together in Shenzhen, in a gathering described as the first of its kind among the leaders of the three powers. Each raised nuclear weapons, but the sources differ on how much Ukraine featured.
p: Donald Trump, Xi Jinping and Vladimir Putin met in Shenzhen, China, during the Asia-Pacific Economic Cooperation summit. Al Jazeera described the encounter as the first time the leaders of the world’s three major powers had gathered together. A French broadcaster reported that Beijing framed the meeting as a way to protect global peace.
Chinese state media said the trilateral talks lasted about an hour and a half. Trump described the three leaders as making history, and on arriving he referred to Putin in warm personal terms.

Putin said the three countries shared a wide range of overlapping interests in settling conflicts, including the full-scale war in Ukraine that Russia launched in 2022. Trump argued that the three were well placed to address nuclear weapons. Xi called for every possible step to head off a nuclear war and said such weapons should be banned outright and eliminated.

Euronews had previewed the summit as focused on disarmament and the conflict involving Iran, and said Ukraine would not be on the agenda. The Guardian’s report of Putin’s remarks suggests the war did come up, so the accounts do not fully line up on what was discussed.

The trilateral followed a separate one-on-one meeting between Trump and Putin set for the same week. It was their first encounter since Alaska in August 2025, when they held high-stakes talks to end the war in Ukraine that did not produce a settlement, according to Al Jazeera.

Meanwhile, Trump’s envoys Steve Witkoff and Jared Kushner were due in Berlin to meet Ukrainian officials and European partners on security guarantees after the war and an economic recovery plan for Kyiv. A US official said the Berlin talks and the China engagements were linked as part of one diplomatic push.
The Guardian reported that Trump has since left China. None of the reports describes any concrete agreement reached at the meeting.
items.cav: The accounts rely on official statements, readouts and Chinese state media, and none gives the full content of the talks. Euronews and the Guardian disagree on whether Ukraine was discussed. The fears of a division of the world into spheres of influence are concerns raised by others, not a confirmed outcome.
items.op: A meeting of three leaders who control the world’s largest nuclear arsenals, with a war in Europe on the table, deserves scrutiny rather than applause for the photo opportunity. Those who negotiate such matters owe the public clear readouts and a plain account of what was agreed. Until they provide one, talk of history counts for little.

items.t: Two-hour ambulance target missed more than 2,000 times in Northern Ireland
items.s: BBC News figures show the two-hour limit on ambulance handovers in Northern Ireland was breached more than 2,000 times in four months. A family’s account of a 12-hour wait has raised questions about the new scheme.
p: In September, 85-year-old William Murphy fell seriously ill at his home in County Down. According to his son Ronnie, the family was told by phone that the ambulance service was “under pressure” and that a crew would arrive as soon as it could. They ended up waiting more than 12 hours, even though a recently launched scheme was meant to free up paramedics more quickly.

That scheme, Release to Rescue, began earlier this year. It caps how long patients can remain in an ambulance parked outside a busy emergency department at two hours, so that crews can get back out to other emergencies. The idea is to stop ambulances being tied up at hospital doors while patients wait to be taken in.

BBC News reported that the two-hour limit was exceeded more than 2,000 times between May and August, the first four full months of the scheme. The Department of Health said the programme had produced “improvements”. It pointed to more than 6,000 waits of two hours or more in the same months a year earlier.

Ronnie said his father’s health worsened while the family waited. When William reached hospital, he needed oxygen because his levels were very low. Ronnie was also unhappy that his father then spent almost two days in the emergency department at the Ulster Hospital before a bed on a ward became available. He said he had no complaints about the care itself, but he described crowded waiting areas, with people sitting and lying on the floor and families visibly distressed.

The Northern Ireland Ambulance Service has apologised to William for the delay after his 999 call. It said demand for its services was greater than its capacity to respond as promptly as it wanted. It also said the protocol had brought some benefits, but accepted that turnaround times needed to fall further. The South Eastern Health Trust said it was sorry to hear about the family’s experience.

Dr Michael Perry of the Royal College of Emergency Medicine said a two-hour limit should not be necessary in a well-functioning system. Ambulances, he argued, could hand patients over straight away if hospitals moved people through in a timely way and departments had space. He warned that winter illnesses would add pressure and told Good Morning Ulster that “real political focus” and a long-term strategy were needed. He said the problem would not be solved quickly and that it was hard to plan without agreeing a budget beyond one year.

Norman Cunningham, a Unite union representative for the NIAS, said that resolving patient flow problems in hospitals would be difficult. The reporting does not say how soon a long-term plan could be agreed or funded.
items.cav: The account of William Murphy’s wait comes from his family and is not independently verified in the reporting. The Department’s claim of “improvements” is set against a different figure, waits of two hours or more a year earlier, so the two sets of numbers may not measure the same thing.
items.op: Patients waiting hours for help deserve clear, published data, not reassurance. A two-hour limit breached thousands of times signals a planning failure, and officials should explain openly what is being done and by when.

items.t: Democrats formally nominate Hakeem Jeffries for House Speaker, putting him on course to be first Black lawmaker to lead the chamber
items.s: House Democrats have formally nominated Hakeem Jeffries to be the next Speaker, a step that puts the New York congressman on course to become the first Black lawmaker to lead the chamber. The full House is due to vote on January 3.
p: Democrats in the US House of Representatives nominated Hakeem Jeffries on Wednesday to be the next Speaker. The full House will vote on January 3, when the new Congress convenes and Democrats take control of the chamber. His election is widely expected.

The nomination was made at a closed-door caucus meeting. The Guardian, citing a source familiar with the tally, reported that Jeffries received 251 of 262 ballots cast. Euronews and the BBC reported 251 votes in favour and 11 against, while DW gave the ballot total as 265. No other lawmaker challenged him. Jeffries told reporters the nomination was “a high honour and a distinct privilege”. He was also re-elected as the party’s leader.

According to the BBC, Democrats will hold at least 257 House seats, well above the 218 needed for a majority, and seven races from the midterm elections remain uncalled. The Speaker is second in line to the presidency after the vice-president. The Guardian reported that Jeffries would preside over the largest Democratic majority in nearly two decades, and that Democrats also won control of the Senate.

The nomination did not pass without dissent. Seven incoming Democrats, including Darializa Avila Chevalier and Claire Valdez, said in a joint statement that their caucus vote was no. They pointed to Medicare for All, immigration enforcement, campaign finance and Gaza as priorities they said constituents had demanded. The group said conversations with Jeffries were ongoing.

Jeffries pledged that House Democrats would fight to lower the costs of groceries, gas and housing, and make healthcare affordable. Euronews quoted him vowing to “hold the crooks accountable”, a reference to planned investigations into Trump officials and his business interests. Euronews also reported that Robert Garcia, the top Democrat on the House Oversight Committee, sent 12 letters asking Trump’s family and senior officials to preserve documents.

The Guardian reported that Jeffries had angered some progressives by refusing to endorse Medicare for All, and that he has recently moved toward their positions on Medicare eligibility. In the Senate, Chuck Schumer faces a challenge from Chris Van Hollen, with a caucus vote scheduled for December 1.
items.cav: Vote totals differ between outlets: 251 to 11 (BBC, Euronews), 251 of 262 (Guardian) and 251 of 265 (DW). Accounts also differ on how long Jeffries has led House Democrats, with France 24 saying since 2022 and others saying since 2023. The Indivisible poll and the Congressional Progressive Caucus statements are reported by one outlet each and are not independently verified.
items.op: A Speaker’s power over what reaches the floor and which inquiries proceed should be exercised in the open. Jeffries’ history-making status matters less than whether he delivers transparent oversight and answers progressives’ demands on the record. Voters want accountability, and that is the standard he should be held to.

items.t: Israel launches ground operation west of Gaza’s Yellow Line, forcing families to flee again
items.s: Israeli forces have launched a ground operation in central Gaza, advancing west of the Yellow Line and pushing Palestinian families from their homes, according to Al Jazeera and DW. The move comes as warnings grow that the ceasefire agreed last year is at risk.
p: Israeli forces have begun a ground operation in central Gaza, moving beyond the line they withdrew to under last year’s ceasefire. Al Jazeera reports that many of the families affected had already been displaced and are now fleeing again.

The Israeli military described the operation as “a precise operation” aimed at removing a threat to its troops. It said the action responded to Hamas ceasefire violations and attempts to rearm. The army has not said how long the operation will last.

Al Jazeera correspondents reported that Israeli tanks and bulldozers advanced towards Salah al-Din Street, Gaza’s main north-south route, near the Nuseirat and Bureij refugee camps. Palestinians fled the area amid heavy gunfire and artillery shelling. The military’s civil affairs body, COGAT, told residents to stay away from the area until further notice.

Palestinian medics told Reuters that one person was killed in an Israeli airstrike in central Gaza, and two more died in separate incidents in Deir al-Balah and Gaza City. Al Jazeera reported further deaths in attacks elsewhere in the enclave.

Hamas called the operation “a flagrant violation of the ceasefire agreement”. Israeli Defence Minister Israel Katz said Israel will not withdraw until Hamas is dismantled, and that forces are prepared to seize more territory if tensions escalate.

The operation comes as the wider plan for Israeli withdrawal, reconstruction and Hamas disarmament has stalled. The United States-backed Board of Peace has warned that the agreement risks collapse. Aid access remains restricted, and the International Organization for Migration says about 100,000 tents are waiting to enter Gaza.

The International Organization for Migration and the World Food Programme warned this week that funding shortfalls and access limits put Palestinian lives at risk. They say more than 1.7 million Gazans are displaced, and that 1.4 million face acute hunger as winter approaches.
items.cav: Casualty figures differ between sources. Al Jazeera cites Gaza’s Ministry of Health at 1,658 Palestinians killed since the ceasefire, while DW cites health authorities at at least 1,600, and the reported Israeli soldier deaths range from five to fewer than 10. Claims by Hamas and Israel about the operation’s purpose remain unverified.
items.op: The ceasefire was meant to open a path to withdrawal, reconstruction and disarmament, and every new operation narrows that path. Civilians who have already been displaced once should not be the price of a dispute between governments and armed groups. Both sides should be asked publicly what this operation achieves and when it will end.

items.t: Israel sends ground forces past Yellow Line into central Gaza, drawing Hamas condemnation
items.s: Israeli ground forces moved into part of central Gaza beyond the Yellow Line on Wednesday after issuing evacuation orders. Hamas says the move breaches the October 2025 ceasefire.
p: Israeli tanks pushed east of the Nuseirat refugee camp on Wednesday, witnesses said, rolling onto Gaza's principal north-south thoroughfare while artillery fire covered their advance. An AFP journalist saw tanks take up positions in the area, which lies in the part of central Gaza held by Hamas.

The Israeli army said the action aimed to take apart a “terror tunnel” west of the Yellow Line, the demarcation that leaves Israel in control of more than 60 percent of the enclave. Military and Shin Bet personnel took part, the army said, and it described Hamas infrastructure in the zone as a threat to its soldiers.

COGAT, the Israeli body overseeing civilian matters in the Palestinian territories, told residents of districts north of the Nuseirat and Bureij camps to move away for their safety. It also closed a stretch of the Salah al-Din road and asked aid groups to stay out of the affected zones.

Hamas responded by calling the incursion a perilous escalation and a clear breach of the truce agreed last October. Both sides routinely trade accusations of breaking the US-mediated deal, which ended two years of fighting.

Video posted by Palestinian outlets and on social media showed households leaving the area. One displaced resident told BBC Arabic that people had abandoned all their possessions, including bedding and clothing. Another described heavy shelling and reported deaths, though these accounts could not be independently verified. Asked about casualties, the army offered only a generic response.

Gaza's civil defence agency, which operates under Hamas, said three men died in separate drone strikes on Wednesday, in Nuseirat, Gaza City and Deir al-Balah. The military said it had hit “terrorists” in the first two and had no knowledge of the third. It remained unclear whether any of the strikes were connected to the ground move.

Health officials in Gaza, also working under Hamas authority, put the death toll since the truce at more than 1,600, a count the UN regards as dependable. The military reports seven soldiers and one contractor killed in the same period. Roughly 1.9 million people remain displaced, and rebuilding has yet to start as Washington's peace proposal has largely stalled.
items.cav: The sources give different figures: BBC reports six Israeli soldiers killed and more than 1,658 Palestinians, while AFP and Euronews cite seven soldiers plus a contractor and more than 1,600 Palestinians. Witness claims about casualties and the army's stated purpose are not independently verified, and any link between the drone strikes and the ground operation remains unclear.
items.op: A ceasefire that both sides accuse each other of breaking cannot be protected by exceptions labelled as limited operations. Israel should publicly explain the specific threat it cites, and civilians ordered to flee with nothing deserve a clear account of what comes next. Without transparency, every incursion erodes the truce and leaves the people of Gaza to pay for it.

items.t: Trump, Xi and Putin’s Shenzhen meeting is a first, but the Guardian sees no progress in it
items.s: A planned meeting of Donald Trump, Xi Jinping and Vladimir Putin in Shenzhen would be the first time the leaders of the US, China and Russia have gathered for talks as a trio, according to a Guardian editorial. The paper argues that the event is a gain for Beijing and Moscow and a setback for Washington and its allies.
p: The Guardian’s editorial board, writing on 18 November 2026, says the meeting is striking but should not be mistaken for an achievement. The talks are due to take place on Thursday in Shenzhen, China, on the sidelines of the Asia-Pacific Economic Cooperation summit. The editorial notes that the gathering has no clear agenda, and argues that the spectacle is effectively the substance.

In the paper’s reading, the event serves the interests of Mr Xi and Mr Putin. Mr Xi is portrayed as a power broker and gracious host in a city that showcases China’s economic and technological ambitions. The editorial contrasts this with a United States that it describes as troubled by tech failures affecting flights and banking. Mr Putin, who had been boasting about the “humiliation” of Europe in the run-up, is said to gain the look of a superpower peer rather than the leader of a pariah state with a struggling economy.

For Mr Trump, the editorial says, the meeting offers a red-carpet welcome and another “first” to promote, which is preferable to headlines about the Republicans’ midterm losses. It argues, however, that his country has less to celebrate. The paper says his tariffs and transactional approach to security have pushed countries such as the Philippines, which hosted the US president on his way to China, into hedging their bets.

The editorial expects little discussion of certain sensitive issues. According to the piece, Mr Trump is not expected to raise Nvidia or suspected Chinese espionage, a choice the paper links to his closeness to Jensen Huang, the chip company’s ousted chief executive. It also suggests the US president is unlikely to press China over its support for Russia’s war against Ukraine, and that Ukraine and Taiwan have reason to be anxious about anything he says to Mr Putin and Mr Xi.

The editorial rejects comparisons with the 1945 Yalta summit, which divided up Europe, as an exaggeration, noting that the meeting is scheduled to last less than an hour. It describes the three governments as having strongly competing interests, despite their surface amity. It says a trade truce followed a Chinese threat over rare earths, but that skirmishes continue. Mr Trump has said he wants to discuss denuclearisation, while the paper notes that China is arming itself quickly, although its arsenal remains much smaller than those of the US and Russia.

The paper stresses that talks between rivals are not inherently unwise. It argues that a carefully prepared trilateral on issues such as disarmament could be productive under a different US leadership, but that this meeting does not fit that model. The sources do not include any official statement of outcomes, so the editorial’s assessment is an opinion about a meeting that had not yet taken place when it was written.
items.cav: This is an editorial opinion, not a news report, and the meeting had not yet taken place when it was published. Claims about the lack of agenda, Mr Trump’s intentions and the state of the US economy and tech sector are the paper’s characterisations and are not independently confirmed in the source.
items.op: Summits without a published agenda ask the public to accept theatre in place of accountability. Smaller states and European allies have a direct stake in what is traded over their heads. Leaders who want credit for a first should be willing to show what they actually agreed.

items.t: Democrats nominate Jeffries for speaker as progressives weigh how far to push him left
items.s: Democrats have nominated Hakeem Jeffries to be the next House speaker, and a Guardian opinion column argues that progressives in the incoming class should press him on Medicare for All, ICE and Israel. The column draws on figures from several other outlets.
p: Democrats nominated Hakeem Jeffries on Wednesday to lead the House once they take control of Congress. According to the Guardian column by Norman Solomon, the choice leaves progressives facing a leader whose record, in the writer's account, is hostile to the left.

The column recalls that Jeffries said five years ago that he would never accept “hard-left democratic socialism.” It notes that at least eight democratic socialists will be among the dozens of progressives entering office, and it urges them to set clear conditions before backing him.

Solomon describes Jeffries’ career as a move from corporate lawyer and state legislator to a House leader who has consistently backed the party’s establishment. He cites reporting by the Intercept and the American Prospect that Jeffries relies heavily on corporate PACs and financial-sector money, a claim the column presents without independent checks.

On healthcare, the column says Jeffries supported Medicare for All as late as 2021. It quotes him on NBC’s Meet the Press this summer saying he is not currently cosponsoring the bill, and says he did not directly answer whether he would hold a floor vote if he became speaker.

The column also says Jeffries has declined to back abolishing Immigration and Customs Enforcement, offering instead a pledge to reform it. It contrasts this with a Democratic National Committee resolution, approved three months earlier, calling for the agency to be abolished.

On Israel, Solomon writes that Jeffries opposed an amendment to block $3.3bn in military aid and that a record 103 House Democrats voted for it the next day. He cites pro-Israel PAC money of $1,741,230 to Jeffries from 2013 through 2024, figures the column attributes to public records and which were not independently verified in the piece.

Solomon reports that Sludge found donations to Jeffries from executives at Anduril and Palantir, and that a Reuters-Ipsos poll from midway through 2025 found 62% of Democrats wanted party leadership replaced. Greg Casar and Alexandria Ocasio-Cortez have both said they would back Jeffries, which the column criticises as premature.

The column closes with Melat Kiros, a 29-year-old attorney and democratic socialist heading to the House from Denver, who said she wants a concrete plan on healthcare, data centres and big tech before supporting any speaker.
items.cav: This is an opinion column by Norman Solomon, not reporting, and many of its figures come second-hand from the Intercept, Sludge, the American Prospect, Reuters-Ipsos and others, none of which are checked here. The evidence does not include a response from Jeffries’ office or from the Democratic leadership.
items.op: Progressives are right to demand clear commitments before handing a leader a gavel. If a speaker’s position on healthcare, immigration and foreign aid is shaped by donors, voters are entitled to know it, and to see those positions tested on the floor. Democrats should answer the questions in public.

items.t: Grand Theft Auto VI launches amid record hype and questions over developer working conditions
items.s: Rockstar’s long-awaited Grand Theft Auto VI is set to go on sale this week, with predictions of record sales. Behind the hype, workers on the game are pressing for union recognition over hours and pay.
p: Grand Theft Auto VI is due to go on sale on Thursday, with the game available to buy from midnight local time. The Guardian reports that gamers in New Zealand are among the first able to download it officially. DW says players can already start downloading the large file a few days before the November 19 release, a process that may take several days depending on connection speed.

The game has been in development for 13 years. According to the Guardian, it cost more than $1bn to make, and some predictions put total sales at 40m copies in its first three months. Its predecessor, Grand Theft Auto V, was the bestselling game of the past decade in the US and reached US$1bn in sales faster than any entertainment product in history, according to the same report.

DW cites figures suggesting that around 10 million people have already bought the game in pre-orders, a claim it presents as a general estimate rather than a verified count. It also says nearly 5,000 people have worked on the project for more than ten years, and that development costs are estimated at around $1 billion, or €900 million.

The launch is being marketed heavily. DW reports that Miami, the real-life inspiration for the fictional Vice City, has received a themed makeover. The local Miami Heat basketball team is due to wear custom Vice City jerseys for a home game, a local festival will feature artists from the game’s soundtrack, and roadside signage has been installed across the area.

Commentators quoted by DW say the series has a broad appeal across generations, from millennials who grew up with earlier instalments to Gen Z players of Grand Theft Auto V. DW also describes the game’s non-player characters as a standout feature, with an estimated 600,000 animations for civilians in the fictional state of Leonida.

DW also notes that the hype could help the wider games industry, which has suffered job losses since the pandemic boom. It estimates that 50,000 people worldwide in the sector have lost their jobs since 2022, though the source does not give a detailed method for that figure.

The Guardian reports that the developers behind the game are campaigning for trade union recognition at the same time as the launch. According to the report, the union push would cover working hours, pay, pensions and parental leave. Former developers have reported extremely long hours and heavy workloads that led to health problems, and trade unions have accused managers of employee surveillance. Rockstar has not been quoted in these reports in the material available here.
The Guardian also invites readers to share their first impressions of the game and whether they plan to take time off work to play it.
items.cav: The 40m sales figure is a prediction, and the 10 million pre-order figure is described only as thought to be the case. The labour allegations come from former developers and trade unions, and the evidence does not include a response from Rockstar. The 50,000 job-loss figure is a worldwide estimate without a clear source.
items.op: A record-breaking launch should not crowd out the people who made it. If a studio’s profits depend on punishing schedules and contested treatment of staff, transparency about working conditions belongs in the launch coverage, not in a footnote. Fans deserve the game, and developers deserve a fair say in how it gets made.

items.t: Bancroft claims whole 2018 squad knew of ball tampering, putting Cummins and Cricket Australia under pressure
items.s: Former Australia opener Cameron Bancroft has said that all players and coaches on the 2018 tour of South Africa knew about the plan to tamper with the ball. His first-person account, which the Guardian reports on, directly challenges the current Test captain Pat Cummins and Cricket Australia’s efforts to close the affair.
p: Bancroft has published a lengthy first-person article in the West Australian that disputes the account of the ball-tampering affair given by Cricket Australia and by its current Test captain. He wrote that the knowledge extended well beyond himself, Steve Smith and David Warner, and that it covered the whole team.

Bancroft said he had not given a complete and truthful account when he was questioned during Cricket Australia’s investigation. He wrote that he withheld details, including when the use of sandpaper began, how long it continued and who else was aware, in order to protect the inquiry and avoid implicating others. He described Cummins’ press conference at the Sydney Cricket Ground as an act of betrayal and said it led him to tell his side for the first time.

According to Bancroft, the idea was raised by Warner during a team discussion at Port Elizabeth, now known as Gqeberha, with then bowling coach David Saker and then head coach Darren Lehmann present. He says Smith joined the conversation briefly and made clear he wanted no part of it. Bancroft also claims that fast bowlers, including Cummins, Mitchell Starc, Josh Hazlewood and Mitchell Marsh, asked him whether his work on the ball was producing enough reverse swing, and that he found their feedback helpful.

Bancroft further alleges that the practice continued into the third Test in Cape Town, where television cameras caught him trying to hide sandpaper in his trousers. He says Saker approached him during the Test at Newlands and told him to do more to make the ball swing, and that Saker later warned against naming sandpaper as the material during the press conference. Bancroft described that account as another lie.

The background is that Bancroft received a nine-month ban, while Smith and Warner were suspended for 12 months. Warner was also barred from leadership roles for life, having been seen as the ringleader. The affair was revived earlier this year when the recently retired Usman Khawaja released an autobiography claiming the knowledge went far beyond those three players. Warner and the 12th man in Cape Town, Chadd Sayers, reportedly backed that version.

Cricket Australia said it would take time to consider Bancroft’s comments and that its forum for players to give confidential testimony would continue, with Bancroft welcome to take part. Cummins’ management said that nothing in Bancroft’s article had not already been answered by Cummins at his press conference, while saying it sympathised with Bancroft.

Cummins, Starc, Hazlewood and Nathan Lyon had earlier issued a joint statement denying any knowledge or involvement, and Cummins repeated that position under questioning. The Guardian also reports that Lehmann left his ABC commentary position early at the final one-day international between Australia and England in Hobart after being told of Bancroft’s claims, and that Marsh did not attend the post-match press conference.
items.cav: Bancroft’s account is his own uncorroborated claim, and the Guardian’s report relies on his article rather than on independent evidence. The earlier denials from Cummins and the other bowlers still stand, and Cricket Australia has not said whether it accepts or disputes the new account. The Khawaja, Warner and Sayers points, and the reactions of Lehmann and Marsh, are second-hand as reported.
items.op: The truth about 2018 matters more than whichever reputation is damaged by it. A confidential forum earns trust only if it is open about who is heard, what is said and what is recorded. Cricket Australia should publish its terms and test every account, Bancroft’s included, against the evidence before anyone’s integrity is settled.

items.t: Xi, Trump and Putin converge on Shenzhen as APEC summit opens, with a three-way meeting set for Thursday
items.s: US President Donald Trump, Chinese President Xi Jinping and Russian President Vladimir Putin were all in Shenzhen for the APEC summit, with a trilateral meeting expected on Thursday. Sources differ in how much they expect from it.
p: Trump landed at Shenzhen Airport on Air Force One on Wednesday, and Xi greeted him there, mirroring a gesture Trump had extended during Xi’s state visit to the US in September. The two leaders then hugged before shaking hands, in what DW described as a highly choreographed arrival.

Trump and Putin also shook hands in the presence of Xi, ahead of the leaders’ welcome banquet. It was their first in-person meeting since August 2025, when Putin was invited to Alaska for talks primarily concerning Russia’s invasion of Ukraine. The handshake follows talks last week in Abu Dhabi involving Russia, Ukraine and European representatives, after which Trump’s negotiating team travelled to the Kremlin to meet Putin.

The Guardian’s diplomatic correspondent Patrick Wintour asks whether the three leaders will carve up spheres of influence in the manner of the Yalta conference, a question the paper frames around the summit’s expected meetings. That is a question, not a report of an agreement.

Trade was also on the agenda. Canadian Prime Minister Mark Carney’s office said he and Trump discussed work towards a trade agreement and agreed to stay in close contact. Mexican President Claudia Sheinbaum said she had a “very good meeting” with Trump and his team and that progress continues on a shared agenda. Washington and Beijing, meanwhile, keep extending a temporary tariff truce, most recently until early January, without a permanent deal.

The chipmaker Nvidia added a new strand to the US-China relationship. Its interim chief executive, Colette Kress, said the company is no longer shipping licensed Hopper data center products to China, the advanced processors that Jensen Huang had persuaded Trump to allow for sale. Kress did not say why shipments had stopped or whether the halt is permanent. Huang resigned last week amid a scandal over alleged Chinese attempts to gain intelligence on the company’s chief executive and to circumvent import restrictions. Beijing calls the espionage allegations unfounded and has threatened to respond in kind if trade restrictions follow.

Japanese Prime Minister Sanae Takaichi also arrived in China for the summit, her first official visit there. Beijing has been upset by her moves to bolster Japan’s military and by her comments last year on Taiwan, which have severely strained bilateral ties.
items.cav: Much of the reporting is live and preliminary, and the outcome of Thursday’s trilateral meeting is not yet known. The Nvidia explanation and the espionage allegations remain unconfirmed claims, and the Guardian’s carve-up question is framing rather than evidence of a deal.
items.op: Leaders may meet privately, but any arrangement touching Ukraine, trade or export controls affects people far beyond the room. Governments should publish what is agreed and why, so that a handshake cannot quietly become a settlement.

items.t: ICJ to rule on The Gambia’s Rohingya genocide case against Myanmar
items.s: The International Court of Justice is set to issue its judgment on Thursday, November 19, in The Gambia’s case accusing Myanmar of genocide against the Rohingya, according to Al Jazeera. DW says the court will be the first to rule on the treatment of the Rohingya in any court.
p: The Gambia brought the case in November 2019, seven years before the expected ruling, and argued that Myanmar had failed its duties under the 1948 Genocide Convention. Al Jazeera adds that the Gambian action was backed by the Organisation of Islamic Cooperation, a body of 57 member states.

The Gambia contends that Myanmar’s forces carried out arson, rape and killings in Rakhine State between 2016 and 2017 with the aim of destroying the Rohingya, in whole or in part. DW reports that a UN fact-finding mission concluded that roughly 10,000 people likely died, and that about 700,000 Rohingya fled to Bangladesh. Al Jazeera puts the number of refugees above 740,000.
